claim: Understanding how climate-mediated biotic interactions shape thermal niche width is critical in an era of global change.
source: Understanding how climate-mediated biotic interactions shape thermal niche width is critical in an era of global change.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of research in the context of global change, drawing on established scientific consensus about climate change impacts.

claim: Most previous work on thermal niches has ignored detailed mechanistic information about the relationship between temperature and organismal performance.
source: Yet, most previous work on thermal niches has ignored detailed mechanistic information about the relationship between temperature and organismal performance, which can be described by a thermal performance curve.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature, based on the authors' review of previous research.

claim: The width of thermal performance curves will be narrower in the presence of interspecific competitors.
source: Here, we develop a model that predicts the width of thermal performance curves will be narrower in the presence of interspecific competitors, causing a species' optimal breeding temperature to diverge from that of its competitor.
evidence: This prediction is derived from a theoretical model developed in the manuscript.

claim: Interspecific competition causes a species' optimal breeding temperature to diverge from that of its competitor.
source: Here, we develop a model that predicts the width of thermal performance curves will be narrower in the presence of interspecific competitors, causing a species' optimal breeding temperature to diverge from that of its competitor.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The divergence in actual and optimal breeding temperatures in Nicrophorus nepalensis is the result of competition with blowflies.
source: We test this prediction in the Asian burying beetle Nicrophorus nepalensis, confirming that the divergence in actual and optimal breeding temperatures is the result of competition with their primary competitor, blowflies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript testing the model prediction.

claim: Intraspecific cooperation enables beetles to outcompete blowflies by recovering their optimal breeding temperature.
source: However, we further show that intraspecific cooperation enables beetles to outcompete blowflies by recovering their optimal breeding temperature.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from group size manipulation experiments.

claim: The ecological niche describes a hyperspace with permissive conditions and requisite resources under which an organism, population, or species has positive fitness.
source: A cornerstone for understanding the distribution and associated ecological impacts of climate change on organismal fitness is the concept of the ecological niche, which describes a hyperspace with permissive conditions and requisite resources under which an organism, population, or species has positive fitness (Hutchinson, 1957; Chase and Leibold, 2003; Colwell and Rangel, 2009).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to foundational ecological literature.

claim: Hutchinson distinguished the fundamental niche from the realized niche.
source: More than a half century ago, Hutchinson (Hutchinson, 1957) distinguished the fundamental niche—characterized by abiotic environmental measures like temperature and precipitation—from the realized niche—characterized by biological interactions like competition and predation.
evidence: This is a historical fact about ecological theory, supported by citation to Hutchinson's work.

claim: The fundamental niche is characterized by abiotic environmental measures like temperature and precipitation.
source: More than a half century ago, Hutchinson (Hutchinson, 1957) distinguished the fundamental niche—characterized by abiotic environmental measures like temperature and precipitation—from the realized niche—characterized by biological interactions like competition and predation.
evidence: This is a definition from ecological niche theory, supported by citation.

claim: The realized niche is characterized by biological interactions like competition and predation.
source: More than a half century ago, Hutchinson (Hutchinson, 1957) distinguished the fundamental niche—characterized by abiotic environmental measures like temperature and precipitation—from the realized niche—characterized by biological interactions like competition and predation.
evidence: This is a definition from ecological niche theory, supported by citation.

claim: Numerous studies have used the relationship between a species' distribution and the climate in which it occurs to estimate a species' fundamental niche.
source: Although numerous studies since then have used the relationship between a species' distribution and the climate in which it occurs to estimate a species' fundamental niche (Kearney and Porter, 2009; Quintero and Wiens, 2013; Gaüzère et al., 2015), a growing number of studies have also employed theoretical, observational, or experimental approaches to evaluate the detailed mechanisms (e.g. physiological limits) (Huey et al., 2012), demographic factors, and species interactions that shape a species' fundamental and realized niches (Monahan, 2009; Nilsson-Örtman et al., 2013; Estay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: A growing number of studies have employed theoretical, observational, or experimental approaches to evaluate the detailed mechanisms, demographic factors, and species interactions that shape a species' fundamental and realized niches.
source: Although numerous studies since then have used the relationship between a species' distribution and the climate in which it occurs to estimate a species' fundamental niche (Kearney and Porter, 2009; Quintero and Wiens, 2013; Gaüzère et al., 2015), a growing number of studies have also employed theoretical, observational, or experimental approaches to evaluate the detailed mechanisms (e.g. physiological limits) (Huey et al., 2012), demographic factors, and species interactions that shape a species' fundamental and realized niches (Monahan, 2009; Nilsson-Örtman et al., 2013; Estay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a characterization of recent research trends, supported by citations.

claim: Differentiating between how abiotic factors and biotic interactions influence niche width is critical for understanding species-specific responses to climate change.
source: In general, differentiating between how abiotic factors and biotic interactions influence niche width is critical for understanding species-specific responses to climate change.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of research approaches, based on logical inference from ecological theory.

claim: The concept of the thermal performance curve was first developed to study how body temperature affects ectotherms' physiological responses and behaviors.
source: The concept of the thermal performance curve (TPC) was first developed to study how body temperature affects ectotherms' physiological responses and behaviors (Kearney and Porter, 2009; Quintero and Wiens, 2013; Gaüzère et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the development of the TPC concept, supported by citations.

claim: The TPC concept has received increasing attention in studies of how warming temperatures influence organismal fitness.
source: Although the TPC concept has received increasing attention in studies of how warming temperatures influence organismal fitness (Clusella-Trullas et al., 2011; Sinclair et al., 2016), it has been developed largely independently from niche-based studies.
evidence: This is a characterization of research trends, supported by citations.

claim: The TPC concept has been developed largely independently from niche-based studies.
source: Although the TPC concept has received increasing attention in studies of how warming temperatures influence organismal fitness (Clusella-Trullas et al., 2011; Sinclair et al., 2016), it has been developed largely independently from niche-based studies.
evidence: This is an observation about the historical development of two research traditions.

claim: Characterizing the TPC is a way to mechanistically quantify a species' thermal niche.
source: Yet, characterizing the TPC is essentially a way to mechanistically quantify a species' thermal niche.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim linking two theoretical frameworks.

claim: The TPC concept is more informative than that of the thermal niche, which is typically defined as the range of temperatures over which organisms occur in nature.
source: Since the TPC describes the detailed relationship between temperature and fitness, the concept may actually be more informative than that of the thermal niche, which is typically defined as the range of temperatures over which organisms occur in nature (i.e. thermal niche width) (Huey and Stevenson, 1979; Hillaert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative evaluation of two concepts, based on logical inference and supported by citations.

claim: The TPC concept describes thermal niche width and quantifies an organism's optimal temperature and how fitness varies with changes in temperature.
source: In other words, the TPC concept not only describes thermal niche width, it also quantifies an organism's optimal temperature and how fitness varies with changes in temperature.
evidence: This is a description of what the TPC concept encompasses, based on the definition of TPCs.

claim: Most TPC studies focus largely on the fundamental TPC and do not explicitly consider biotic interactions.
source: In contrast, most TPC studies focus largely on what amounts to the fundamental TPC and do not explicitly consider biotic interactions (Dillon et al., 2010; Gunderson et al., 2016; Swaddle and Ingrassia, 2017).
evidence: This is a characterization of the TPC literature, supported by citations.

claim: The few TPC studies that have considered biotic interactions have almost all focused on predator-prey interactions.
source: The few TPC studies that have considered biotic interactions have almost all focused on predator-prey interactions (Ockendon et al., 2014; Gibert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a characterization of a subset of the TPC literature, supported by citations.

claim: No study has differentiated between fundamental and realized TPCs.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no study has differentiated between fundamental and realized TPCs, nor experimentally quantified a species' realized TPC in the context of interspecific competition, despite the fact that ecologists have long acknowledged that interspecific competition is a key driving force shaping a species' realized niche (Schoener, 1983; Eurich et al., 2018; Freeman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about a gap in the literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: No study has experimentally quantified a species' realized TPC in the context of interspecific competition.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no study has differentiated between fundamental and realized TPCs, nor experimentally quantified a species' realized TPC in the context of interspecific competition, despite the fact that ecologists have long acknowledged that interspecific competition is a key driving force shaping a species' realized niche (Schoener, 1983; Eurich et al., 2018; Freeman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about a gap in the literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: Ecologists have long acknowledged that interspecific competition is a key driving force shaping a species' realized niche.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no study has differentiated between fundamental and realized TPCs, nor experimentally quantified a species' realized TPC in the context of interspecific competition, despite the fact that ecologists have long acknowledged that interspecific competition is a key driving force shaping a species' realized niche (Schoener, 1983; Eurich et al., 2018; Freeman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about established ecological theory, supported by citations.

claim: A few studies have shown that intraspecific cooperation can help social species expand their realized niche width.
source: Furthermore, although a few studies have shown that intraspecific cooperation can also help social species expand their realized niche width (Sun et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2019), little is known about how intraspecific cooperation influences the realized TPCs of social organisms.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing research, supported by citations.

claim: Little is known about how intraspecific cooperation influences the realized TPCs of social organisms.
source: Furthermore, although a few studies have shown that intraspecific cooperation can also help social species expand their realized niche width (Sun et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2019), little is known about how intraspecific cooperation influences the realized TPCs of social organisms.
evidence: This is a claim about a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Burying beetles rely on vertebrate carcasses for reproduction.
source: Burying beetles (Silphidae, Nicrophorus) are ideal for investigating how social interactions influence both fundamental and realized TPCs because the potentially antagonistic effects of interspecific competition and intraspecific cooperation on the realized TPC can be studied simultaneously. Burying beetles rely on vertebrate carcasses for reproduction and often face intense intra- and interspecific competition for using these limiting resources (Pukowski, 1933; Scott, 1998; Rozen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about burying beetle biology, supported by citations.

claim: Burying beetles often face intense intra- and interspecific competition for using vertebrate carcasses.
source: Burying beetles rely on vertebrate carcasses for reproduction and often face intense intra- and interspecific competition for using these limiting resources (Pukowski, 1933; Scott, 1998; Rozen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about burying beetle ecology, supported by citations.

claim: Competition for carcass access is temperature-dependent because blowflies are more abundant and active at higher ambient temperatures.
source: Competition for carcass access is temperature-dependent because the beetle's main competitors, blowflies (family Calliphoridae), are more abundant and active at higher ambient temperatures (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the temperature-dependence of competition, supported by citation.

claim: Blowfly maggots grow faster and digest carcasses more quickly at higher temperatures.
source: Blowfly maggots also grow faster and digest carcasses more quickly at higher temperatures (Donovan et al., 2006; Kotzé et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about blowfly biology, supported by citations.

claim: Cooperative carcass preparation and burial enables beetles to outcompete blowflies and expand their thermal niche to warmer environments.
source: Previous studies have shown that cooperative carcass preparation and burial enables beetles to outcompete blowflies and expand their thermal niche to warmer environments (Sun et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the effects of cooperation, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis without interspecific competitors in the laboratory is 15.6°C.
source: Accordingly, we found that the beetle's optimal breeding temperature or fundamental TPC—defined as the mean temperature at which breeding success was highest (calculated from our GLM)—was 15.6°C.
evidence: This is a finding from laboratory experiments, calculated from statistical models of the data.

claim: The probability of N. nepalensis breeding successfully changed unimodally with ambient temperature in the laboratory.
source: We first explored N. nepalensis's fundamental breeding TPC in a controlled lab environment. We found that the probability N. nepalensis breeding successfully changed unimodally with ambient temperature (Figure 3a, GLM, χ²2 = 26.29, p < 0.001, n = 117).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Beetles had a greater likelihood of flying at 16°C while running at a stable speed on the treadmill.
source: We found that beetles had a greater likelihood of flying at 16°C while running at a stable speed on the treadmill (Figure 3b, GLM, χ²2 = 13.22, p = 0.001, n = 72).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of treadmill experiments and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: N. nepalensis took less energy to raise its body temperature enough to begin flying at 16°C than at other temperatures.
source: In other words, N. nepalensis took less energy to raise its body temperature enough to begin flying at 16°C than at other temperatures (Figure 3c and d, GLM, χ²2 = 23.18, p < 0.001, n = 29).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temperature difference data, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: In the presence of interspecific competitors (blowflies) in the wild, the optimal breeding temperature (realized TPC) of N. nepalensis was roughly 13.1°C.
source: As predicted by our model, in the presence of interspecific competitors (blowflies) in the wild, the optimal breeding temperature (i.e. the realized TPC) of N. nepalensis was roughly 13.1°C, which is lower than the optimal temperature in the lab in the absence of blowflies (i.e. the fundamental TPC) (Figure 4a, GLMM, χ²2 = 16.56, p < 0.001, n = 343).
evidence: This is supported by field experimental data and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis in the presence of blowflies (13.1°C) is lower than the optimal temperature in the lab in the absence of blowflies (15.6°C).
source: As predicted by our model, in the presence of interspecific competitors (blowflies) in the wild, the optimal breeding temperature (i.e. the realized TPC) of N. nepalensis was roughly 13.1°C, which is lower than the optimal temperature in the lab in the absence of blowflies (i.e. the fundamental TPC) (Figure 4a, GLMM, χ²2 = 16.56, p < 0.001, n = 343).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results from different conditions.

claim: When excluding blowflies in the field, the optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis increased to approximately 14.6°C.
source: Intriguingly, when excluding blowflies and removing the threat of intraspecific competition in the field, the optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis increased to approximately 14.6°C, such that the realized TPC began to approach the fundamental TPC in the absence of blowflies, ultimately becoming broader than when in the presence of interspecific competitors (Figure 4b, GLMM, χ²2 = 16.08, p < 0.001, n = 175).
evidence: This is supported by field experimental data with blowfly exclusion, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The realized TPC of N. nepalensis became broader when blowflies were excluded in the field compared to when in the presence of interspecific competitors.
source: Intriguingly, when excluding blowflies and removing the threat of intraspecific competition in the field, the optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis increased to approximately 14.6°C, such that the realized TPC began to approach the fundamental TPC in the absence of blowflies, ultimately becoming broader than when in the presence of interspecific competitors (Figure 4b, GLMM, χ²2 = 16.08, p < 0.001, n = 175).
evidence: This is a comparison of TPC widths under different experimental conditions, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: N. nepalensis in cooperative groups had an optimal breeding temperature (realized TPC) of 15.6°C.
source: We found that N. nepalensis in cooperative groups had an optimal breeding temperature (i.e. realized TPC) of 15.6°C, which is identical to their optimal temperature from the fundamental TPC in the lab.
evidence: This is supported by group size manipulation experiments in the field.

claim: The optimal breeding temperature of N. nepalensis in cooperative groups (15.6°C) is identical to their optimal temperature from the fundamental TPC in the lab.
source: We found that N. nepalensis in cooperative groups had an optimal breeding temperature (i.e. realized TPC) of 15.6°C, which is identical to their optimal temperature from the fundamental TPC in the lab.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results showing convergence of realized and fundamental TPCs.

claim: The optimal breeding temperature of solitary pairs of N. nepalensis was 14.1°C.
source: In contrast, the optimal breeding temperature of solitary pairs was 14.1°C, similar to that of the realized TPC of 14.6°C in the field (Figure 5, group size × temperature interaction, χ22 = 6.84, p = 0.033, n = 328; for large groups, χ22 = 9.40, p = 0.009, n = 162; for small groups, χ22 = 18.42, p < 0.001, n = 166).
evidence: This is supported by group size manipulation experiments, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Beetles that cooperate are able to expand their realized TPCs such that they converge on their fundamental TPCs.
source: These results suggest that beetles that cooperate are able to expand their realized TPCs such that they converge on their fundamental TPCs, whereas those do not cooperate have divergent realized and fundamental TPCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the group size manipulation results.

claim: Beetles that do not cooperate have divergent realized and fundamental TPCs.
source: These results suggest that beetles that cooperate are able to expand their realized TPCs such that they converge on their fundamental TPCs, whereas those do not cooperate have divergent realized and fundamental TPCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the group size manipulation results.

claim: If thermal specialist species compete with thermal generalist species adapted to higher temperatures, the optimal performance temperature of specialists will decrease.
source: Our theoretical model suggests that if thermal specialist species compete with thermal generalist species adapted to higher or lower temperatures, the optimal performance temperature of specialists will decrease or increase, respectively.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: If thermal specialist species compete with thermal generalist species adapted to lower temperatures, the optimal performance temperature of specialists will increase.
source: Our theoretical model suggests that if thermal specialist species compete with thermal generalist species adapted to higher or lower temperatures, the optimal performance temperature of specialists will decrease or increase, respectively.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Blowflies force the beetle's optimal breeding temperature lower and the realized TPC narrower.
source: Our empirical results examining competition between burying beetles (thermal specialists) and blowflies (thermal generalists) for access to carcasses support this theoretical prediction, finding that blowflies force the beetle's optimal breeding temperature lower and the realized TPC narrower.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical findings from the experiments.

claim: The mechanism that enables cooperative beetles to expand their range to lower elevations relative to non-cooperative beetles is their ability to align their fundamental and realized thermal niches.
source: Therefore, the mechanism that enables cooperative beetles to expand their range to lower elevations relative to non-cooperative beetles (Sun et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020) appears to be their ability to align their fundamental and realized thermal niches.

claim: The realized TPC extends the realized thermal niche concept by considering how abiotic factors additionally indirectly affect fitness by driving biotic interactions like species competition.
source: Thus, the realized TPC extends the realized thermal niche concept, which only considers the temperature ranges in which a species can occupy or breed successfully (Huff et al., 2005; Rehfeldt et al., 2008) by considering how abiotic factors (i.e. climate) additionally indirectly affect fitness by driving biotic interactions like species competition.

claim: Allee effects will likely occur in N. nepalensis in warmer environments.
source: We predict that Allee effects—when higher population density has a positive effect on individual fitness and population growth rate until it reaches the maximum (Allee, 1931; Courchamp et al., 1999; Stephens and Sutherland, 1999)—will likely occur in N. nepalensis in warmer environments.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings and ecological theory, supported by citations.

claim: When a low temperature specialist species competes with a high temperature generalist species, the optimal temperature of the realized TPC of the thermal specialist shifts towards a lower temperature.
source: We began by addressing how interspecific competition influences the realized TPC of a focal species, finding that when a low temperature specialist species (e.g. burying beetle) competes with a high temperature generalist species (e.g. blowfly), the optimal temperature of the realized TPC of the thermal specialist shifts towards a lower temperature and the width of the TPC decreases (Figure 2b).
